name: Asymptotic growth
section: State the function and the model
quick: Comparison of functions at all sufficiently large inputs.
definition: An eventual growth claim ignores a finite initial range but must hold at every allowed later input. Specify the size parameter and function before giving a bound.
example: Changing only the value at n=1 does not change an eventual growth classification.
confusion: Finite experiments do not establish a statement about every later input.

name: Cost model
section: State the function and the model
quick: A specification of what work is counted and how input size is measured.
definition: A function counting comparisons differs from one counting bit operations. An algorithmic bound is meaningful only relative to the specified operations and size parameter.
example: Copying n elements counts n writes if one operation writes one element.
confusion: One line of code may perform work that grows with its operands.

name: Unit-cost model
section: State the function and the model
quick: Each specified basic operation has a fixed cost.
definition: A unit-cost analysis counts defined actions, such as a comparison or one element access, as constant work. Check whether that model fits the representation.
example: A loop with n fixed-cost body operations and fixed-cost control has linear cost.
confusion: Arbitrary-length integer arithmetic need not have constant bit cost.

name: Positive integers
section: State the function and the model
quick: $\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$ in this lesson.
definition: Input sizes n here are positive integers unless another domain is explicitly stated. Zero is excluded from this convention for N.
example: n=1 is allowed; n=0 needs an explicitly extended domain.
confusion: Some books use N to include zero; read the stated convention.

name: Big O
section: Big O: an eventual upper bound
quick: One fixed positive multiple eventually bounds the function above.
definition: For eventually nonnegative f and positive comparison g, $f=O(g)$ means some c>0 and integer n0 satisfy $0\leq f(n)\leq cg(n)$ for every n at least n0.
example: $3n+5\leq8n$ for n at least 1 proves $3n+5=O(n)$.
confusion: The multiplier cannot be chosen anew for each input.

name: Threshold
section: Big O: an eventual upper bound
quick: An input after which an inequality must always hold.
definition: The integer n0 may exclude a finite beginning. Once chosen with the multiplier, it stays fixed as n varies.
example: $n^2\leq2n^2-5n$ holds from n0=5 onward.
confusion: A large threshold cannot excuse arbitrarily late failures.

name: Tight growth bound
section: Big O: an eventual upper bound
quick: Matching upper and lower bounds using the same comparison function.
definition: Fixed positive multiples may differ, but both bounds must hold beyond one threshold. Big Theta records this information.
example: $4n^2\leq4n^2+2n+9\leq15n^2$ gives a tight quadratic bound.
confusion: A valid upper bound can be much larger than the function.

name: Big Omega
section: Big Omega and Big Theta
quick: One fixed positive multiple eventually bounds the function below.
definition: The notation $f=\Omega(g)$ means some c>0 and threshold n0 make $0\leq cg(n)\leq f(n)$ hold for all later allowed n.
example: $3n^2+5n+7\geq3n^2$ proves a quadratic lower bound.
confusion: Omega is a direction of bound, not a synonym for best case.

name: Big Theta
section: Big Omega and Big Theta
quick: The function is eventually between two fixed positive multiples of the comparison.
definition: There exist positive c1,c2 and an integer threshold n0 with $0\leq c_1g(n)\leq f(n)\leq c_2g(n)$ for every n at least n0.
example: $n\leq2n+1\leq3n$ for n at least 1 gives $\Theta(n)$.
confusion: Theta does not assert exact equality or equal values at small inputs.

name: Pointwise operations on functions
section: Useful rules, with reasons
quick: Apply the operation to values at the same input.
definition: For functions sharing a domain, f+h has value f(n)+h(n), and max(f,h) has the larger value at n. The input is sometimes omitted for readability.
example: If f(n)=n and h(n)=2, then (f+h)(n)=n+2.
confusion: The symbol naming a function is not a fixed numeric constant.

name: Little o
section: Strictly slower growth
quick: Every positive multiple of the comparison eventually bounds the function above.
definition: For each positive epsilon, choose a threshold after which $0\leq f(n)\leq\varepsilon g(n)$. The threshold may depend on epsilon.
example: $n=o(n^2)$ because choosing n0 at least 1/epsilon makes $n\leq\varepsilon n^2$.
confusion: Big O needs one multiplier; little o needs every positive multiplier.

name: Epsilon
section: Strictly slower growth
quick: $\varepsilon$ is a positive real multiplier chosen arbitrarily.
definition: The Greek letter epsilon expresses “however small a positive multiplier is requested.” A later threshold may depend on its value.
example: With epsilon=1/100, proving f at most epsilon g means f is at most one hundredth of g after the threshold.
confusion: Epsilon is not automatically zero or one particular tiny number.

name: Strict growth comparison
section: Strictly slower growth
quick: $f\prec g$ means $f=o(g)$ in this lesson.
definition: Read it as f grows strictly more slowly than g. It abbreviates the little-o definition, not a pointwise inequality at every input.
example: $n\prec n^2$ even though both equal 1 at n=1.
confusion: The same glyph has an order-relation meaning elsewhere; this entry is specifically about growth.

name: Binary search
section: Doubling and halving
quick: Search a sorted list by repeatedly discarding an impossible half.
definition: Compare a middle item with the target. Sorted order identifies which half may still contain the target; repeat on that interval.
example: Halving an eight-item interval repeatedly produces sizes about 4,2,1.
confusion: The sorted-order and access-cost assumptions matter.

name: Worst-case cost
section: Worst case is a different axis
quick: The maximum cost among inputs of a fixed size.
definition: Select the greatest cost for each size n to obtain a function, then bound that function using O, Omega, or Theta.
example: Linear search may inspect all n entries when a target is absent.
confusion: A worst-case lower bound need not apply to every input.

name: Best-case cost
section: Worst case is a different axis
quick: The minimum cost among inputs of a fixed size.
definition: Select the least cost for each size before analyzing growth. Upper and lower asymptotic bounds can both describe this function.
example: Linear search stops after one comparison when the first item matches.
confusion: Big Omega does not mean best case.

name: Expected and average-case cost
section: Worst case is a different axis
quick: A probability-weighted average over inputs of each size.
definition: A probability distribution assigns input probabilities totaling one. Multiply each input’s cost by its probability and add to define the expected cost.
example: For two equally likely costs 2 and 6, the expected cost is 4.
confusion: No unspecified “typical input” determines a unique average.

name: Linear search
section: Worst case is a different axis
quick: Check items in order until a match is found or the list ends.
definition: The cost depends on the position of the first match or on absence. With fixed-cost comparisons, the best case is constant and worst case linear in list length.
example: Finding the third item takes three comparisons.
confusion: Linear search does not require sorted input, unlike binary search.

name: Subsequence
section: Irregular functions still use the definitions
quick: Selected terms of a sequence kept in their original order.
definition: Even-indexed and odd-indexed terms are examples. An eventual bound must hold on every such part after its single threshold.
example: If f(n)=n on evens and n squared on odds, the two subsequences have different behavior.
confusion: A bound verified only on one subsequence need not hold on the whole sequence.

name: Bit length
section: Recurrences and input size
quick: The number of binary digits in a positive integer without leading zeros.
definition: A positive N has $b=\lfloor\log_2N\rfloor+1$ bits, so $2^{b-1}\leq N<2^b$. Numeric magnitude and representation length are different size measures.
example: 1000 lies between 512 and 1024, so it has ten binary digits.
confusion: A loop of N iterations is exponential in bit length even though linear in N.

name: Arbitrary-precision arithmetic
section: Recurrences and input size
quick: Store as many digits as the calculation needs.
definition: Unlike a fixed-width integer, this representation can grow. Operations on longer operands may require more work in a model counting individual bit operations.
example: Adding two b-bit integers processes their digits and possible carries.
confusion: No fixed numeric range does not mean constant operation cost.
